question: I'm applying from India for a German student visa. Do I need an APS certificate?
answer: Generally yes: for a German student visa applied for in India, an APS certificate is mandatory unless an exemption applies [S2]. You are exempt if: you will obtain a non-German degree in Germany; you plan PhD/postdoc studies; you have a scholarship/stipend from German or EU public funds; or your studies build on a non-Indian school certificate (e.g. International Baccalaureate) or a non-Indian degree (e.g. British Bachelor) [S2]. If you are exempt, you must instead upload recognition of your school-leaving certificate, either an anabin confirmation or a ZAB Statement of Comparability [S7]. Universities may also require APS for admission: TUM, for example, requires it for applicants with an Indian school or university degree [S5]. Your visa category also matters: APS-requiring degree applicants book at VFS, and an appointment in the wrong category will not be accepted [S1]. This is not legal advice; please confirm with the German mission in India.

question: What kind of account do most international students use to prove they can pay for their studies in Germany?
answer: Most international students use a blocked account, called a "Sperrkonto", as proof of funds, with the money shown as a credit to the account [S1]. Key conditions: a Sperrkonto only allows a certain level of withdrawals each month, and you can only close it with approval from an embassy/consulate or the competent foreigners authority [S1]. The German embassy in India's checklist states the account must hold sufficient funds for your first year, currently €11,904, with no more than €992 withdrawable per month [S4]. Sperrkonten are available from a range of providers, and the DAAD recommends getting advice from the German embassy or consulate [S1]. Alternatives include a formal obligation letter ("Verpflichtungserklärung") from a sponsor living in Germany or proof of a German/EU scholarship [S4]. Please confirm current requirements with your embassy or consulate, as rules can change; this is not legal advice.

question: If I finish a degree in Germany but need time to find a job, how long can I stay on the post-study permit?
answer:
After you successfully finish your studies in Germany, your residence permit can be extended by up to 18 months so you can look for a job that matches your degree [S6][S2][S5]. You apply for this extension at your local Foreigners Registration Department (under § 20 Para. 1 No. 1 AufenthG) [S6].

Key conditions:
- Your studies count as finished once the university certifies in writing that you passed your last exam, so keep that confirmation letter or envelope with its postmark [S6].
- You must prove you can cover your living costs and that you have health insurance [S2][S3].
- During the 18 months you may do any job, including internships or self-employment [S3][S2].
- Any stay abroad longer than six months ends the permit unless you agree on it in writing beforehand [S3].
- If you find a suitable job, you can get a residence permit for employment [S2].

This is not legal advice; please confirm with your local Foreigners Registration Department.

question: While I'm on the 18-month job-search permit after graduating in Germany, am I allowed to work?
answer: Yes. During the job-search period of up to 18 months after graduating in Germany, you are allowed to work without restriction [S2][S3][S4]. You can take any job, and it does not have to be related to your degree [S2]. This includes internships and trainee posts, and you may also work self-employed or as a freelancer while you search [S4]. Key conditions: you must prove that you can cover your living expenses and that you have health insurance [S2][S4]. A stay abroad of more than six months (e.g., an internship abroad) automatically ends the permit unless you have agreed otherwise in writing with the Foreigners Registration Department [S4]. Note: this is different from the 'Chance card', which limits work to 20 hours per week [S7]. This is general information, not legal advice; please confirm your situation with your local Foreigners Registration Office (Ausländerbehörde).

question: In Germany, should I usually book a specialist directly, or start with a general doctor?
answer: Usually, start with a general practitioner (GP, Hausarzt). The GP is the first point of contact for mild illnesses and decides whether you need a specialist [S3][S5]. If so, you get a referral to book a specialist appointment [S7]. Exceptions: for some fields you can book directly without a referral, for example a dentist, gynaecologist or orthopaedist [S7][S2]. If you already know your illness needs a specialist such as a dermatologist, you can contact them directly [S1]. Practical tips: specialist appointments can take weeks or more than a month [S7]. Mention your type of insurance when booking, since private practices may not be covered by statutory insurance [S7]. On weekends, use an on-call clinic (Bereitschaftspraxis) or call 116 117. In emergencies, go to hospital or call 112 [S5][S8]. This is general information, not legal or medical advice; check with your insurer.

question: Can a student residence permit in Munich cover a required preparatory language course before a full-time degree?
answer: Yes. In Munich, a residence permit for the purpose of studying also covers preparatory measures, including attending a preparatory language course [S1]. The key condition is that you already have a guaranteed place on a full-time degree programme at the relevant educational institution [S1]. If you only have conditional admission or another form of preparatory study, granting the permit is at the discretion of the Service Centre for Immigration and Naturalisation [S1]. Berlin's guidance similarly counts a preparatory language course as part of the study purpose when admission to the degree is tied to attending that course [S3]. If you don't have a guaranteed place, a separate study-preparation permit exists; it requires a university entrance qualification or a conditional offer and is limited to a maximum of 18 months for a preparatory language course [S2]. This is not legal advice; please confirm your situation with Munich's Service Centre for Immigration and Naturalisation.

question: What should I do at Sabancı after submitting my Turkish residence permit file, and who decides the outcome?
answer: After you hand your file to the IRO, it is sent to the Istanbul Provincial Immigration Administration, and you should regularly check the e-ikamet website for updates, since the result (within 30–90 days) comes to you by email/SMS and the website, not to the IRO [S1]. Card approval and preparation can take up to 90 days; the card goes to the address on your address document, and tracking it is your own responsibility [S1]. If you listed the Tuzla Campus, the Communication Center will receive it and notify you [S1]. Once you get the card, send a copy to irolegal@sabanciuniv.edu and studentinfo@sabanciuniv.edu [S1]. Leaving Türkiye before the evaluation is not recommended, as it may lead to rejection [S6]. The Directorate General of Migration Management decides the outcome; the university only guides you and submits your file [S1][S6]. The rules can change, so please confirm any decisions with the immigration authority; this is not legal advice.

question: Does my student residence permit in Türkiye automatically let my parents live there too?
answer: No. Your student residence permit does not automatically give your parents or other relatives the right to live in Türkiye [S1][S8]. According to the Presidency of Migration Management, your student permit does not entitle your parents or other family members to any right to obtain a residence permit through you; however, they may apply separately for their own residence permit if they meet the conditions [S8]. The sources do not explain which permit type or conditions would apply to your parents, so check this directly with the Presidency of Migration Management (or your local Provincial Directorate of Migration). This is general information, not legal advice; rules can change.

question: How soon after getting a residence permit card should I register my address at Sabancı?
answer:
You must register your address within 20 days of receiving your residence permit card [S1]. If your address changes later, you must register the new address too [S1]. Erasmus and Exchange students can skip this step if they will not extend their permits in Turkey [S1].

Key conditions and steps:
- Book an appointment through the Immigration Office Appointment System; you need e-devlet access, and you must attend in person on the appointment day [S1].
- You must be over 18, your card must be active, and you must be in İstanbul [S2].
- If you live in the university dormitories or in Tuzla, Pendik, Kartal, Maltepe, Şile, Adalar or Kadıköy, register at the Pendik District Immigration Office [S2].

This is general guidance, not legal advice; confirm details with the Immigration Office or the IRO.

question: If I want to use Turkish GSS as an international student, how long after university registration do I have to apply?
answer: You have three months: you must apply for General Health Insurance (GSS) within three months after your university registration [S1][S2]. Sabancı University specifies this means your first registration to the university, and that you apply after receiving your foreign national ID number, at the Social Security office (SGM) for the district where you live [S4]. If you miss this 3-month legal period, you cannot benefit from GSS afterward [S3][S4]. One exception: if you change your program or program level (e.g. undergraduate to master's), you may apply again [S3]. Note a slight difference: METU tells its students to apply within three months of the first day of Fall semester classes, rather than from registration [S6]. So check which date your university and local SGK office use. This is not legal advice; these processes are run by state bodies and can change, so confirm the deadline with SGK or your university [S3].

question: Are private health insurance policies in Türkiye accepted at every hospital?
answer:
No. Private health insurance policies in Türkiye are not accepted at every hospital. They are only valid in hospitals where the insurance company has a contract [S1][S3]. The insurer must have an agreement with the hospital, so you may not be able to use your policy everywhere [S2]. Private policies only cover services at contracted hospitals and only within the limits in the policy [S4]. Keep in mind:
- Coverage is limited, and your limit goes down with each procedure you have [S2].
- The policy may not cover all costs [S2].
- Expensive private hospitals can use up your limit quickly [S2].

Before you go, check whether the hospital is contracted with your insurer. Reading an English copy of your policy also helps [S4]. This is general information, not legal advice; confirm details with your insurer or the responsible authority.

question: Do all foreign students in Türkiye have to pay the residence permit document fee, or are some nationalities exempt?

Students coming under agreements or exchange programmes to which Türkiye is a party get a short-term residence permit without paying a fee [S7]. One source mentions Türkiye Scholarships students paying the document fee during extension applications, which suggests students may still pay it [S3]. The sources do not say whether any nationalities are exempt from either fee, so that part of your question is not covered. For current fees, the sources point to www.goc.gov.tr [S2]. question: What kinds of housing can an international student look at in Türkiye?
answer: You have four main housing options in Türkiye: university dormitories on campus, state dormitories run by KYK (Higher Education Credit and Hostels Institution) in various parts of the city, private dormitories, or an apartment you rent in the city [S2]. Private dormitories are found around most campuses; they usually offer better facilities (e.g. newer furniture) than state dormitories, but cost more [S1]. Renting is also common: many students share a house with a few friends, especially in neighbourhoods close to universities [S1]. Rents vary by city, location and the features of the home [S1]. Homes are typically apartments with a large living room, 2 to 4 bedrooms, a separate kitchen and often a balcony, heated by a central system or a combi boiler [S1]. Check current options and prices with your university or the housing provider before deciding.

question: Does a Turkish student residence permit itself give me permission to take a paid job?
answer: No. Your student residence permit does not automatically give you the right to work in Türkiye; you need an official work permit [S1]. Key points: - You cannot apply for a work permit yourself: you first find a job, then the employer applies for you [S1]. - Associate/undergraduate students can work only after their first year of study [S3], for part-time jobs [S1], and weekly working hours may not exceed 24 [S5]. - Graduate students can get a work permit from their first year, for full-time or part-time jobs [S1]. - Per METU, work permits for students are only for jobs outside the university/campus [S1]. - Working without a work permit can lead to cancellation of your residence permit [S4]. - While your work permit is valid, it counts as a residence permit [S4]. This is not legal advice; confirm with the Migration Office or the Ministry of Labour and Social Security.

question: If I apply for Turkish GSS after the three-month deadline, can I assume I will still be covered retroactively?
answer: No. The sources do not support assuming any coverage after a late application; they say that if you miss the 3-month window, you lose the right to GSS entirely. You must apply within three months of your university registration [S2][S3]. If you don't apply within this period, you will not have the chance to apply again, and you cannot benefit from this right later [S3][S1]. Even when you do apply on time, you can only use health care services after the first 30 days of activation [S5]. If you miss the deadline, you must get an annual private health insurance covering inpatient and outpatient treatment instead [S6]. One exception: if you change your program or program level (e.g. undergraduate to master's), you may apply again [S1]. Note that METU counts the deadline from the first day of Fall classes [S5], while other sources count it from registration [S2][S3]. Confirm your situation with SGK (hotline 170) [S5]. This is not legal advice.

question: Is the Turkish student residence permit card fee 810 TL or 964 TL?
answer: The sources give different figures. METU states that students applying for a student residence permit pay only the card fee, 964.0 TL for 2026 [S1]. Sabancı University tells you to bring more than 810₺ in cash to pay [S5]. However, that page doesn't say which year its amount applies to, and it notes the fee changes annually [S5]. METU's figure is explicitly dated 2026, so it is the more current one. As a student, you don't pay visa or residence permit fees, only the card fee [S1]. You can pay online at dijital.gib.gov.tr using the accrue number (tahakkuk numarası) from your online application [S1]. Keep the original receipt, because you must hand it in to the Immigration Office [S5]. Fees can change, so please confirm the current amount on your own application document or with the immigration authority [S6].

question: Does the German student visa checklist for Indian applicants require a passport with just one blank page?

question: I'm 29 and studying in Germany. Roughly how much is statutory student health insurance per month?
answer:
The sources give different figures, roughly €110 to €140 per month for the public (statutory) student rate while you are under 30. All were retrieved on the same date (2026-11-18), and none is clearly marked as the most current:

- About €120–130 per month for the reduced student rate if you are under 30 [S1].
- Around €110 per month, according to the DAAD practical guide [S2].
- About €140 per month until age 30 [S5].
- A German embassy visa sheet budgets €137 per month for insurance costs when it calculates the funds you must show for a visa [S3].

Because you are 29, plan for your next birthday. Once you turn 30, you must pay the standard contribution, even if you are still studying [S1]. One source says this is €250 or more per month [S5]. At that point, private insurance may be cheaper [S1].

This is not legal advice. Please confirm current rates with a statutory insurer.

question: If I want to stay and look for work after graduating, how do the options in Germany and Türkiye compare?
answer:
Germany offers a longer job-search period right after graduation, while Türkiye offers a shorter but extendable one.

Germany: you can apply for a residence permit under § 20 Para. 1 No. 1 AufenthG for 18 months to look for a job [S4]. This option is only available immediately after graduation [S4]. If you first take a job abroad, you can instead request a 12-month 'Chance card' visa, but it does not let you work without restriction [S4]. In general, a German degree usually lets you join the labour market directly [S3].

Türkiye: graduates of Turkish universities can get a one-year residence permit to seek a job [S6]. You must apply for a short-term residence permit within six months after graduation, under the "those who graduated from a Turkish university" category [S6]. It can be extended for one more year if you apply before it expires or within 90 days after [S6]. Campus career fairs and career centres can help [S1].

This is not legal advice; confirm with the immigration authority.

question: Do student assistant jobs at my university count toward my work-day limit in Germany?
answer: Generally no. On-campus jobs (student/research assistant work) at universities and other academic institutions come in addition to the 140-day rule and have no time limit under the Residence Act [S6][S5]. Research or academic assistants have no limit on days worked [S4][S2]. Key conditions: • You must still inform the immigration office (Foreigners' Office) [S2][S4]. TUM says you need the Foreigners' Office authorization in your residence permit for this [S5]. • The 20-hours-per-week limit during lecture periods still applies for social security purposes, and your university may have its own weekly hour limits [S6]. • If you're unsure whether a job counts as on-campus, ask your Foreigners Registration Department office [S3]. This is general information, not legal advice, so please confirm with your local Foreigners' Office.

question: Does my student residence permit let me work in Germany, and is it the same in Türkiye?
answer:
Your sources don't say whether a German student residence permit allows you to work. They only explain that non-EU students must apply for a residence permit for the purpose of studying at the foreigners' office [S4]. Please check work rights with the German foreigners' office.

In Türkiye, your student residence permit does not by itself let you work. You need an official work permit [S2][S3].
- **Who applies:** You first find a job, and the employer applies for the permit for you [S2].
- **Undergraduates:** You can get a permit only after your first year, only for part-time jobs, and only for jobs off campus [S2].
- **Graduate students:** You can get a permit from your first year, for full- or part-time jobs, but only off campus [S2].
- **Compulsory internships:** These need a work permit exemption [S6].
- **Risk:** If you work without a permit, your residence permit could be canceled [S1].

This is not legal advice, so please confirm with the responsible authority.
